respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise depuis le grec (zoo7/5g), verification humaine requise

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo7/5g.xml (edition Bekker/Ruelle, Open Greek and Latin / First1000Years of Greek, CC BY-SA 4.0), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Seul le Livre 10 (« Epitome physicorum »), le plus riche en contenu zoologique direct des 38 livres du Problemata (comparaisons systematiques entre l'homme et les boeufs, chevres, moutons, chevaux, chiens, porcs, oiseaux, etc. sur la physiologie et le comportement), est traduit dans cette premiere etape ; les 37 autres livres restent a traduire et seront ajoutes progressivement, livre par livre. Le decoupage en sections numerotees suit exactement la structure TEI de la source (67 sections pour ce livre ; chaque section source correspond a un paragraphe de cette traduction).

div.p: Why do some creatures cough and others not, for instance man coughs but the ox does not? Is it because in most animals the residue turns to some other use, but in man it turns this way? Or is it because man has the largest and moistest brain, and coughing occurs when phlegm flows down from it?

Why does blood flow from the nostrils in man alone among the animals? Is it because he has the largest and moistest brain, from which the veins, filled with the residue, send forth their flow through the passages? For diseased blood becomes thinner than pure blood, and this is blood mixed with the residues of the brain, being like a kind of serum.

Why are some animals fat beneath the flesh, others fat throughout the flesh, and others both? Is it that in those with dense flesh, the moisture is held back between skin and flesh, since the skin stands apart from it by nature, and this moisture, being concocted, becomes fat; while in those with looser flesh and a skin lying close upon it, the fat forms throughout the flesh; and those with both conditions grow fat in both ways?

Why do children and women have less vitiligo (white skin-blotches) than men, and among women the older ones have it more? Is it because vitiligo is an escape of breath, and children's bodies do not breathe easily, but are dense, and women's less so than men's, since it turns instead to the menstrual flow? The smoothness of the skin shows its density. But the bodies of older men and women breathe more easily, for, like old buildings, they alone have their parts standing apart in their composition.

Why does man alone of the animals get vitiligo? Is it because he has the thinnest skin of all animals, and is at the same time the most given to breath? A sign of this is that vitiligo occurs first and most in the thinnest-skinned parts. Or is it for this reason, and also because he alone among animals goes grey? For grey hairs occur where there is vitiligo, so that it is impossible for creatures that do not go grey to have vitiligo.

Why do goats and sheep, though not of the greatest bodily size, yield the most milk when milked, while man and the ox yield less, proportionally? Is it because in the latter the surplus is spent upon the body, while in the former, the goats and the sheep, all the residue left over becomes milk? Or is it because they bear more young than the larger animals, so that they draw off more of the residue for the nourishing of more offspring? Or is it that, owing to the weakness of their bodies, more residue is produced in them when they are pregnant? For milk comes from the residue.

Why do some animals, when they change their water, change their colour and come to resemble the creatures of that place, as goats do, while others do not, as man does not? And in general, why do some change and others not, as the raven does not change? Is it that those whose nature does not master the moisture, as is the case with birds (which is why they have no bladder), do not change? And why is it not the creatures themselves but their offspring that change? Is it because the young are weaker than their parents?

Why are the males, as a general rule, larger than the females? Is it because they are hotter, and heat promotes growth? Or because the males are complete and the females as it were maimed? Or because the one is brought to completion in a long time, the other in a short one?

Why do some animals give birth quickly, while others have a long gestation? Is it because the longer-lived are by nature slower to reach completion? Long-lived creatures are indeed slow to give birth. Yet not the very longest-lived: the horse, for instance, is slower to give birth than man, but shorter-lived. The cause of this is the hardness of the womb; for just as dry earth does not quickly bring forth crops, so it is with the womb of the horse.

Why do the offspring of other animals resemble their parents' nature more than human children do? Is it because man's soul is affected in many different ways through intercourse, and, according to however the father and mother happen to be disposed, the offspring too are correspondingly varied? Most of the other animals, however, are disposed toward this one single end; and moreover, they are for the most part not satisfied through this desire in the way man is.

Why are white men and white horses generally grey-eyed? Is it because, there being three colours of eyes — black, goat-coloured, and grey — the colour of the eye follows the colour of the body, and this correspondence is grey-eyedness?

What is the cause of dwarfism? And, more generally, why are some creatures altogether large and others small? There are two causes: either the place, or the nourishment. The place, if it is confined; the nourishment, if it is scant — just as men, working on creatures already born, try to make them small, as those do who raise little dogs in quail-cages. Those, then, for whom the place is the cause become pygmy-like: for they come to have the breadth and length proper to the size of their parents, yet are altogether small. The cause of this is that, on account of the narrowness of the place, straight lines, bent back upon themselves, become curved; so that, just as figures painted small in tavern-signs are nonetheless shown having breadth and depth, the same happens with pygmies. But those who are stunted through lack of nourishment appear to have childish limbs. And one may see some that are very small indeed, yet well-proportioned, like Maltese lap-dogs; the cause here is that it is not the place, but nature, that has worked upon them thus.

Why are some animals born from one another, while others are formed from certain combining substances, having, in a similar way, an origin from the beginning, just as those who discourse on nature say that the original generation of animals itself came about, through the changes and great upheavals of the cosmos and the universe as a whole — and now, if this is to happen again, must not similar motions occur? For the beginning of every work is the greatest part of it, being as it were half the whole; and the seed is a beginning. Now for the small creatures that are not born from one another, the cause of their coming into being just as they did at the beginning is the smallness of their seed; for the smaller the thing, the smaller its beginning too, so that even the changes affecting such a creature suffice to generate its seed for it, which is indeed what happens: they arise chiefly amid such changes. But the larger creatures require a greater change as well.

Why are some animals prolific of young, such as the pig, the dog, and the hare, while others are not, such as man and the lion? Is it because the former have many wombs and many chambers, which desire to be filled, and into which the seed is divided, while the latter have the opposite?

Why does man have the smallest distance between his eyes, in proportion to his size, of all animals? Is it because he is the most according to nature of all creatures, and perception is by nature directed forward? For one must look ahead toward that in the direction of which one moves. The greater the distance between the eyes, the more the sight will be directed sideways. If, then, the eyes ought to be placed according to nature, the distance between them ought to be as small as possible; for thus one will look most directly forward. Furthermore, the other animals, since they have no hands, must look somewhat to the side; wherefore their eyes are set further apart, especially in sheep, because they make their way chiefly with their heads bowed down.

Why do some other animals not have nocturnal emissions at all, while others have them rarely? Is it because none of them lies on its back, and nothing that does not lie on its back has such emissions? Or is it that the other animals do not dream in the same way, and the emission occurs together with imagination?
Why do some animals move their heads, while others do not? Is it because some do not have a neck? Wherefore these do not move the head.

Why does man sneeze more than any other animal? Is it because he has wide passages through which breath and smell enter? For when these are filled with breath, sneezing occurs. That they are wide is shown by the fact that man has the least keen sense of smell of all the animals; for the more finely made passages give more exact perception. If, then, into wide passages the moisture — whose being turned to breath produces the sneeze — enters both more abundantly and more often, and men have such passages more than any other animal, it is reasonable that they should sneeze most often. Or is it because their nostrils are the shortest in length, so that the heated moisture can quickly become breath, whereas in other animals it is first cooled owing to the length of the passage?
Why is no animal's tongue fatty? Is it because the fatty is dense, while the tongue is by nature porous, so that it may perceive flavours?

Why do the females urinate with a straining effort, but not the males? Is it because the female bladder lies further away, both in depth and in length? For the womb lies between the seat and the bladder in females, so that what is expelled requires greater force, owing precisely to this distance from the womb; and it is forced out by straining together with the breath.

Why do all animals that do not fly shed their winter coat, except the pig? For the dog sheds it, and so does the ox. Is it because the pig is the hottest of animals, and its hairs grow from heat? For fattiness is of such a nature. Now the other animals shed their hair either because the moisture is chilled and falls away, or because their own natural heat is unable to concoct the nourishment, or, in the case of the pig, because its moisture suffers nothing untoward — since its nourishment is well concocted — and so it does not shed its hair. For wherever the cause of shedding lies, sufficient fattiness is able to prevent it. Sheep and men are unaffected because of the quantity and density of their hair; for the cold does not penetrate to a sufficient depth to either freeze the moisture or hinder the concoction by the heat.

Why, when plucked, do sheep's hairs grow back softer, but men's harder? Is it because sheep's hairs grow from the surface? Wherefore they are pulled out without pain, the source of their nourishment, which lies in the flesh, remaining undamaged; the residues, then, evaporate more once opened up, while the wool draws its own proper nourishment from the flesh — and flesh is nourished on what is soft and sweet. But men's hairs, growing from deep within, are pulled out by force and with pain, as is shown by the fact that they draw blood; the place, then, being wounded, comes also to be scarred, wherefore this happens in the end to those who are plucked; but so long as hairs grow back, they grow back hard, because all the nourishing part of the flesh has failed there, and they now arise from residues instead. A sign of this: in all peoples toward the south the hair is hard, because the external heat, penetrating to a depth, evaporates the well-concocted nourishment; whereas among those beneath the Bears (the north) it is soft, for in them both the blood and the sweet humours lie nearer the surface, wherefore they are also fair of complexion.

Why do sheep's hairs, the longer they grow, become harder, while men's grow softer? Is it because sheep's hairs, having the kind of nourishment described, hang far from their source and are thus less nourished, and the nourishment present in them readily evaporates under the heat owing to its good concoction? And as they dry, they become drier still, for moisture is what makes hair soft. But men's hairs are fewer, yet nearer their source; they are better concocted because of being fewer, and concoction makes hair softer, for all concocted things are softer than unconcocted ones. Man's hair, indeed, comes from a greater amount of residue than sheep's wool. A sign of this: young sheep have softer wool than old ones.

Why are hairy men and hairy birds lustful? Is it because they are hot and moist by nature, and both these qualities are needed for mating: heat causes secretion, moisture is what is secreted. For the same reason lame men too are lustful; for their nourishment, being scant, reaches the lower parts but little on account of the disability of their legs, and instead comes in abundance to the upper region and is compounded into seed.
Why has man no mane? Is it because he has a beard, so that the nourishment for such a residue, going there instead, passes to the jaws?

Why do all animals have an even number of feet? Is it because motion is impossible unless something is at rest, unless the creature leaps? Since, then, motion in walking must consist of two things, motion and rest, these two are already an even number. And four-footed creatures have more feet because they move two and rest on two, and six-footed creatures likewise; and the rest have two more again, of which one moves and the other rests.

Why do hairs grow from the scars of horses and asses, but not of men? Is it because in other animals the skin is part of the flesh, but in man it is, as it were, an affection of the flesh? For it seems that in them the surface, being chilled, becomes more solid, just as the so-called "crust" that forms on boiled flour does. Since, then, that crust too is boiled flour, what is called man's skin would likewise be flesh. Now when a man is wounded or chafed, it happens that his flesh becomes denser; wherefore, the surface flesh having been altered, the wounds do not take on the same nature as they had from birth; and, it being altered, it is no wonder that nothing further grows from it, just as with the so-called fox-manges (alopecia), which are likewise corruptions and alterations of the surface flesh. But in beasts of burden, when they are chafed and then healed, the diseased parts of the body are filled in again, being the same in kind, though weaker than they were at first. And since their skin too is a part of them, hairs would form and grow there too (for hairs grow from skin); but they grow white, because the skin has become weaker than it was originally, and white hair is the weakest kind of hair.

Why in other animals do twins survive equally well whether male and female, but not in man? Is it because in man twins are especially weak, since he normally bears but one at a time? And it is contrary to nature for a male and a female to occur together as twins in him, so that what is most contrary to nature is also weakest.

Why do hairs grow from the scars of horses and asses, but not of men (repeated)? Is it because the scar hinders it, either through its density or by destroying the nourishment? In men it hinders it altogether, owing to the weakness of the hair; in horses it did not hinder it, but only impaired it.

Why do animals have an even number of feet? Is it because everything that moves must have something at rest, and this could not happen if the feet were odd in number — which is what motion, according to the corresponding placement of the feet, in fact was?

Why do animals sleep for a shorter time than they are awake, though not continuously? Is it because not all the residue is concocted at once, but whenever some part is concocted, being thereby lightened, the creature wakes? And those wake more often in whom the region that concocts the residue is cold; for it ceases quickly and often, and this cessation is waking. That sleep is pleasant, though this seems unlikely, appears to be because it is a rest. But even so, rest does not last longer than activities according to nature in this either; nor, even if eating is pleasanter than not eating, do creatures nonetheless spend more time eating than not eating.

Why do some animals follow their parents immediately, while others do so late, or with difficulty, or never — as man does? Is it because some quickly acquire the power of recognition, while others do so late? And some are without perception of what benefits them, while others have such perception. Those, then, that have both of these — I mean both the perception of what benefits them and the completion of the body — follow; those lacking either do not do this, for both capacities are needed, the power to move and the power to perceive.

Why does vitiligo not occur in other animals? Is it because in others it is a disease, but in men their skins and hairs become patchy white? But even so one might be puzzled why it does not occur later in life in other animals, but the mottling is present from birth. Is it because the skins of other animals are hard, while man is by nature the thinnest-skinned of all? Vitiligo is an emission of breath, which is prevented from escaping in other animals by the density of their skin.

Why does grey hair occur together with vitiligo, yet wherever there is grey hair, there is not always vitiligo? Is it because hairs come from the skin, and greyness is a kind of decay of the hairs? Whenever, then, the skin is affected, the hair, being derived from it, must of necessity be affected too; but when the hair is affected, the skin need not be.

Why are some animals fierce after giving birth, such as the dog and the pig, while others show no evident change, such as woman and sheep? Is it because those full of residue become gentle? For what causes distress departs at the birth. But in those from whom the removal is taken from a body in good condition... so that leanness produces irritability through the resulting condition, just as hens are not fierce when they have not laid, but become so when brooding, on account of their fasting.

Why do eunuchs, though in most other respects changing toward the female — for they acquire a woman's voice, its shrillness, and its lack of definite pitch, and change as thoroughly as castrated creatures do among other animals — nonetheless, contrariwise, bulls and rams acquire larger horns when castrated, because the females of these species are the opposite of the males in this respect? Wherefore some, on being castrated, come to have greater horns, others lesser. In size alone do eunuchs change toward the male; for they become taller. But this belongs to the male; for females are smaller than males. Or does not even this belong to the male, but rather to the female? For it is not toward every kind of size, but only toward length, that they change, while the male changes toward breadth and depth as well; for that is when it is fully mature. Furthermore, as the female stands to the male, so within the female herself the maiden stands to the woman; for the one is already fully formed, the other not. It is toward the condition of these, then, that the eunuch changes; for their growth is in length. Wherefore Homer well said, "pure Artemis granted her height," as though, through her virginity, she were able to give what she herself possessed. The eunuch, then, does not change toward the male in respect of size; for he does not change toward completeness. But eunuchs do increase in length.

Why do eunuchs either altogether fail to get, or get less, varicose veins? Is it because in their castration they change their nature toward the barren? Such are the boy and the woman, neither of whom gets varicose veins, except a woman rarely.
Why does man utter more different sounds than other creatures, which, though not differing in kind among themselves, utter but one? And man too has but one voice, yet many dialects.

Why is this voice different in man, but not in other animals? Is it because men articulate many letters, while of other creatures some articulate none, and some only two or three of the consonants? These, together with the vowels, make up dialect. Speech, however, does not consist merely in signalling by voice, but by voice's affections, such as that one is in pain or is glad; the letters are affections of the voice. Both children and beasts show this alike; for children too do not yet articulate the letters.

Why does man alone of the other animals become a stammerer? Is it because he alone can also be mute, and stammering is a kind of muteness? But indeed this part is not even fully developed in animals at all. Or is it because man alone shares in reason, while other creatures share only in voice? Stammering is not, as the name might suggest, a single defect, nor is it merely an inability to speak continuously.

Why is man born lame from birth more than any other animal? Is it because other animals have strong legs? For four-footed creatures and birds have legs of bone and sinew, while man's are fleshy; on account of this softness, then, they are the more readily impaired in movement. Or is it because man alone among animals has a gestation of many possible lengths? For he is born at seven months, eight months, or ten months. Other animals have one fixed time for completion, without lingering; but in man there is much time spent while still numerous within the womb, so that, being soft, and being moved, their extremities are broken more, the longer the time.

Why do eunuchs have ulcerous and rotting shins? Is it because women do too, and eunuchs are womanish? Or is this merely incidental, and the true cause, which applies to women as well, is that their heat rushes downward? Their menstrual discharge shows this. This is also why neither eunuchs nor women grow hairy, on account of their great moisture.

Why does no animal but man suffer from stone? Is it because in beasts of burden and many-hoofed creatures the passages of the bladder are wide? And those creatures that at first do not, but later bear their young alive within them, such as some fish, none of these has a bladder at all, but such sediment is instead compressed into their belly, as with birds too, so that it passes quickly out through the vent. But man both has a bladder and a narrow neck to it, relatively to its size. Because he has this part, then, the earthy matter is compressed into the bladder — wherefore chamber-pots are stained by it — and because of the heat of the place it is further concocted and thickened, and it remains and grows on account of the narrowness of the urethra; for the earthy sediments, unable to pass out easily, turn back upon one another and become a stone.

Why do beasts of burden not belch, nor oxen and horned animals, nor birds? Is it on account of the dryness of the belly? For the moisture is quickly used up and filtered through; belching occurs when it remains and turns to breath. In crested (long-necked) animals, on account of the length of the neck, the breath rushes downward, wherefore they break wind especially. Birds and horned animals do neither. Nor do cud-chewing animals belch, because they have many stomachs and the so-called honeycomb-stomach; the breath's passage, then, both up and down, occurs through many parts, and the moisture is used up before it can be turned into breath and produce either a belch or a sound.

Why is it that all tame animals also exist as wild ones, but not all wild ones are also found tame? Even men, it seems, are found wild somewhere, and dogs among the Indians, and horses, and elsewhere too; but lions are not found tame, nor leopards, nor vipers, nor many others. Is it because it is easier for something inferior both to come into being from the beginning and to change into that state? For nature is not effortless in achieving the ultimate perfection straightaway, though the first stage may come more readily. Wherefore all things, even the tame kinds, are at first wilder rather than tame, as is a child, or a man who is omnivorous and lives by passion — but these are weaker. So it is with the works of art as well as of nature. For in these too all things are for the most part poorly made, and the poor examples are more numerous — a bed, a garment, or anything else. And what is beautiful may always be taken to be, in some sense, also poor, but what is poor is not all also beautiful — as one may see, examining the works of the ancient painters and sculptors; for there was never anywhere a truly excellent painting or statue, but all were poor. In the same way, nature too makes all things poorly, and more of them, and in greater numbers, but excellent ones more rarely, and cannot achieve it in every case. The tame is the better, the wild the poorer. It is not by its first, original nature, but by the nature toward which, I think, it tends, that it more easily produces the excellent and tame. The opposite kinds either never, or with difficulty, and only in certain places and times, or under some particular blending of the whole, do all animals become tame. The same holds for all plants too: whatever kinds are tame also occur wild, but not all can be tamed; yet nonetheless, in their own proper region, being suited to many things in a particular way, they grow, even neglected and wild, better and tamer than those cultivated elsewhere.

Why do men have large navels, while in other animals they are not conspicuous? Is it because in the others, since they remain within for a long time, the navels wither and are drawn out straight, and the whole wound swells over, wherefore some navels are indeed rather ugly? But man is born incomplete, so that his navels remain moist and full of blood, in keeping with this. That some are born complete and others incomplete is shown by the fact that some are at once able to live on their own, while human infants need care.

Why do some animals mate but once, others many times, and some at a fixed season of the year, others whenever it happens; man always, but wild creatures not often; and the wild pig once, the tame pig often? Is it on account of nourishment, warmth, and exertion? For Love thrives in abundance. Moreover, the same creatures in one place give birth once, in another more often — sheep, for instance, in Magnesia and Libya give birth twice. The cause is the long duration of gestation; for when full, the creature does not desire, just as full creatures do not desire food. And pregnant creatures desire mating less, because the purgation does not occur.

Why are men with widely-spaced teeth generally short-lived? Is it because this is a sign that the bone is dense, so that the brain, being unable to breathe easily, is weak, and, being moist by nature, quickly putrefies? For other things too, when not moved and not allowed to give off vapour, decay. Wherefore man's head is the hairiest part, and the male is longer-lived than the female because of the sutures. But one should examine this also in other creatures.

Why are those whose palm-line runs all the way through longer-lived? Is it because the unjointed parts are the shortest-lived, as with aquatic creatures? If, then, the unjointed are short-lived, clearly the jointed are the opposite. Such are those in whom even the parts naturally unjointed are especially jointed; and of the hand, the inner part is the least jointed.
Why is man alone, or chiefly, of the animals subject to squinting? Is it because he alone, or chiefly, is susceptible to it in infancy, when squinting happens to all?
Why is man most affected by smoke among the animals? Is it because he weeps the most, and being affected by smoke goes together with weeping?

Why does a horse delight in and desire a horse, and man a man, and in general do like creatures desire their like? For it is not, surely, because every animal is beautiful, and desire is of the beautiful; for then the beautiful ought to be pleasant. But as it is, not every beauty is pleasant, though the beautiful and the pleasant... nor for everyone is pleasure or beauty the same; eating or drinking is pleasanter to one, and love-making to another. Why each creature, mating with its own kind, finds it especially and most pleasurably erotic, is a different problem; but that it is thereby also most beautiful is not true. Rather, we think what is pleasant for intercourse is beautiful, because, desiring, we take pleasure in seeing it. And indeed it is the same with other desires too; for the thirsty see the drink as pleasanter to look at. What is beautiful in relation to some particular need, then — that which we most desire — seems pleasantest, whereas what is beautiful in itself is no longer so regarded. A sign of this: men too seem beautiful to us when we look at them with a view to intercourse. Is it, then, in such a way that we take more pleasure looking at them than at things unrelated to intercourse? Nothing prevents this, unless we happen not to be desiring. In the same way a drink seems more beautiful too: if we happen to be thirsty, we shall see it with more pleasure.

Why is it that in man the fore parts are hairier than the hind, while in four-footed creatures the hind parts are hairier? Is it because all two-footed creatures have hairier fore parts? For birds are in the same condition as man. Or is it that nature is always accustomed to cover the weaker parts more, and each part is in some way weak? Now in all four-footed creatures the hind parts are weaker than the fore, on account of their position; for they are more liable to suffer from cold and heat. But in man the fore parts are weaker, and have suffered the same thing.

Why does man sneeze more than any other animal? Is it because he catches cold in the head more than any other? The cause of this is that, the heat about the heart being naturally inclined to rise upward, in other animals its natural course is toward the shoulders, and from there, by reflection, splits, part going toward the neck and head, part toward the spine and loins, since all these lie along the same straight line, parallel to the animal's stance. Moving thus, the heat distributes the body's moisture evenly among these parts too, for moisture follows heat. Wherefore four-footed animals do not catch cold in the head much, nor do they sneeze much; for sneezing is either a sudden rush of breath, when the moisture evaporating is somewhat more than usual, or a rush of unconcocted moisture. It occurs, then, before catarrhs, which do not happen to other animals, because in them the flow of heat is distributed evenly forward and backward. But man, standing upright upon his base, like a plant, has his greatest and most vehement flow of heat directed toward the head. Travelling there, it rarefies and heats the passages around it; being of this kind, they become more receptive of moisture than the passages below the heart. Whenever, then, it happens that they become moister than is fitting, and are chilled, the heat is driven from outside inward, and, having its nourishment there and being drawn together within, grows; and growing, it is carried toward the head and the passages within it; into these the moisture follows, being thin and unconcocted, and fills them, producing catarrhs, and sneezes likewise. For at the onset of catarrhs, the heat, carried up ahead of the moisture and turning the passages to breath, produces sneezes both by the expulsion of breath and by the preceding rise of the moisture, which is thin and sharp. Wherefore it also happens that, together with the sneezes of a head-cold, watery matter is blown from the nose. And when all these movements have set out, the connected and affected moisture settles upon them and blocks the passages about the head and nose; for, becoming swollen and distended, it produces the pains about the head. A sign of this is that no breath escapes either outward or through them; wherefore those with a head-cold neither sneeze nor smell. Those who sneeze without a head-cold do so from the same causes, but from small and slight beginnings, so that the moisture, gathered together with the heat and turned to breath by it on account of its small quantity, falls in through the nostrils. And the noise of the breath is caused no less by the violence of its passage than by its quantity; for when the heat is carried directly against the brain and strikes upon it, it is reflected toward the nostrils, because the passages there stretch outward from the brain. Since, then, the breath's passage toward the nostrils occurs contrary to its natural course, owing to this reflection, it becomes violent; wherefore it produces the noises. Among the other animals, birds are especially subject to catching cold in the head, because they are most similar in shape to man; yet they suffer it less than man, because most of them hold their heads low, since their feeding is from the ground.

Why are sea creatures larger and better nourished than land creatures? Is it because the sun, consuming what surrounds the land, takes away its nourishment? Wherefore creatures kept enclosed are better nourished too. From all this, then, sea creatures are exempt.
Why do other animals take dry food more often than moist, while man takes moist food more often than dry? Is it because man is by nature the hottest of creatures? He therefore needs the most cooling.

Why do eunuchs not go bald? Is it because they have an abundant brain? This comes about in them because they do not have intercourse with women; for seed proceeds from the brain by way of the spine. For this same reason, castrated oxen too seem to have large horns once castrated. The same cause seems to explain also why women and children are not bald.

Why can some creatures nourish themselves on their own immediately after birth, while others cannot? Is it those that are shorter-lived that are receptive of memory? Wherefore all such creatures also die sooner.

Why does the other animals produce excrement more dry than moist, while man produces it more moist than dry? Is it because these animals use dry food more, while man uses moist food more than dry? All residue comes from nourishment, and more residue from more nourishment. Some animals, then, use moist nourishment more, others dry, because some creatures are by nature dry, others moist. Those that are by nature dry desire the moist more, since they are deficient in it, while those that are by nature moist desire the dry more, being deficient in that instead.

Why are birds and men, and the more courageous of animals, harder-fleshed? Is it because spirit goes together with heat? For fear is a chilling. Those, then, whose blood is warm are also courageous and spirited; and blood is nourishment. And whatever plants are watered with warm water all become harder.

Why do the four-footed creatures that are not large bear monstrosities most, while man, and the large creatures such as horses and asses, do so less? Is it because these — dogs, pigs, goats, sheep — are far more prolific than the large animals, some of which bear only one at a time, most others generally so as well? Monstrosities arise when the seeds overlap and become mixed together, either as they issue forth, or in the mingling that occurs within the female's womb. Wherefore birds too produce them; for they lay twin eggs. Monstrosities come from twins whose yolk is not divided by its membrane.

Why is the human head hairier than the rest of the body, and disproportionately so, while in other animals the opposite holds? Is it because in others too, some, from excess of nourishment, produce teeth, some horns, some hair? Those that produce horns have less hairy heads, since the material is spent there; those that produce teeth have hairier heads than the horned creatures (for these have a mane), but less hairy than such creatures as birds. For birds have the same condition as men: what in them is spent variously, owing to abundance, this in man is spent upon the head; for man has neither the one nor the other so abundantly as to be spent everywhere.

Why does man alone of the animals go grey? Is it because most animals shed their hair every year, such as the horse and the ox, while some do not shed it, but are short-lived, like the sheep and others, whose hair, as it were, does not age, and so does not turn grey either? But man neither sheds his hair nor is short-lived, so that with time he goes grey.

Why are those in whom the parts below the navel are larger than those toward the chest short-lived and weak? Is it because the belly is cold on account of its smallness, so that it is not good at concocting, but productive of residue? And such creatures are sickly.

Why are some animals generated not only from one another but also spontaneously, while others are generated only from one another, as man and the horse? Is it, if for no other reason, because for the former the time of generation is short, so that the generative season does not overrun it, and it is possible for generation to occur within a single change of season, whereas for the latter, generation greatly overruns it — for they take a year, or ten months? So that it is necessary either that they be generated spontaneously... or be generated from one another.

Why are the teeth of the Ethiopians white, and whiter than others', while their nails are not likewise? Is it that the nails are not, because the skin too is black, and blacker than others', and the nails grow from the skin? But why are the teeth white? Is it because whatever the sun draws the moisture from, without staining it, becomes white, as with wax? The skin, then, it stains, but the teeth it does not stain; rather, the moisture is evaporated from them by the heat.

Why do some creatures die at once or quickly when the head is removed, while others do not? Is it that this happens to those that are bloodless and require little nourishment? For such creatures do not quickly need nourishment, nor is the heat poured into them along with moisture, without which it is impossible for blooded creatures to live; but for these it is possible, for they are able to live far longer without breathing. The cause of this has been stated elsewhere.
